messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 51
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Tax Inspector
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 39

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Feeling Tired: Feeling very tired or exhausted, Discomfort: Feeling uncomfortable, Unpredictability: Unpredictable situations
  Threat: False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Memory: Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear, Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
  Negative Appraisals: No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore, Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person, Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Minh Tran is a 51-year-old Vietnamese American man who works as a tax inspector for a regional government office. He has been married for eleven years to his current wife and presents to therapy with a PCL-5 score of 39, describing a constellation of symptoms that have quietly reshaped the architecture of his daily life over the past several years. He came to the intake appointment wearing a collared shirt buttoned to the top, and he chose the chair in the far corner of the room before the clinician had a chance to direct him to a seat.

The trauma Minh describes occurred within a previous long-term relationship, with a woman he had been with for nearly seven years. He characterizes those years as ones in which the violence escalated so gradually that he had difficulty, even in retrospect, identifying when it began in earnest. What he can describe with precision is a particular evening in the kitchen of the apartment they shared — an argument that began over something trivial, a missed phone call, and then the sound of a ceramic mug shattering against the wall beside his head. What followed was not an isolated incident but a sustained period during which he was shoved, struck, and on at least two occasions thrown against furniture. He stayed. He has spent considerable time trying to understand why, and has arrived at an explanation that offers him little comfort: he trusted her completely. She was, he says, the person he had organized his life around. The betrayal he feels is not abstract — it lives in the specific memory of her voice, which could shift without warning from warmth to violence, and it is that unpredictability, the impossibility of reading what was coming, that marked him most deeply.

In the months after the relationship ended, Minh threw himself into his work. Tax inspection suited him — structured, rule-governed, predictable. But the symptoms he had managed to outpace began catching up with him. Fragments of memory from those evenings would surface without invitation: not full scenes but shards — the particular angle of light in that kitchen, the sensation of a grip on his forearm — appearing suddenly and then dissolving before he could examine them. There are portions of what happened that he cannot retrieve at all, no matter how deliberately he tries, and this troubles him in a way he finds difficult to articulate, as though the gaps themselves are evidence of something he is not permitted to know about himself.

At work, Minh conducts audits that require him to visit businesses and offices across the city. These visits are, by nature, unpredictable — new environments, unfamiliar people, rooms he has never been in before. He has developed a habit of pausing in doorways before entering, scanning the room, and positioning himself so that his back is against a wall. His colleagues have noticed. One of them made a joke about it at a team lunch, and Minh laughed along, but he did not change his behavior because to him it does not feel like a choice. He also finds himself checking over his shoulder when he walks between buildings, a reflex he cannot suppress even when he is certain, on a rational level, that nothing is wrong. He will react to a door slamming two offices away as though the sound were directed at him personally — a surge of alertness that takes minutes to subside.

What has become harder to manage is the exhaustion. On days when fatigue accumulates — long audits, difficult clients, disrupted sleep — he finds himself more raw, more easily startled, more prone to the intrusive fragments. He has come to understand tiredness not as a neutral physical state but as a kind of vulnerability that he cannot afford.

Minh describes his inner life with a flatness that suggests long familiarity with disappointment. He has come to believe that nothing genuinely good is available to him anymore, and when asked to elaborate, he says simply that he feels more like a function than a person — someone who processes paperwork and pays bills and occupies space, but who is not quite real in the way other people seem to be. What finally brought him to seek help was his wife, who told him, carefully and without accusation, that she could not reach him. He is afraid she is right. What he hopes for, he says, is less to feel better than to feel like himself again — though he is no longer entirely sure who that is.
